{"id": "68:24/q03", "question": "What did the owners resolve by saying no poor person should enter?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:24/q03/p1", "position": "They meant to keep poor people out of the garden that day and deny them any of its harvest.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Muqātil, Ibn Qutayba, Yaḥyā ibn Sallām in Māwardī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī and Ṭabrisī give the exclusion as their private resolve. {"id": "68:24/q08", "question": "What do reports say about the garden's owners and their decision?", "turns_on": "The reports vary in the owners' provenance, the number and conduct of the sons, and whether the place is specified.", "positions": [{"id": "68:24/q08/p1", "position": "They were Ethiopian sons who called their charitable father foolish and vowed to exclude the poor after his death.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima, reported by Ṭabarī, says their father fed the poor from his garden. {"id": "68:26/q05", "question": "What did they mean by 'We are astray'?", "turns_on": "Whether the destroyed orchard made them think they had taken a wrong road, or they already recognized moral error; the moral readings differ over excluding the poor, straying from truth, and ingratitude.", "positions": [{"id": "68:26/q05/p1", "position": "They thought they had lost the road and arrived somewhere other than their garden.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Qatada as reported by Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tabari, al-Jishumi, al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, and Ibn Abbas as reported by Ibn Kathir and al-Durr give the wrong-road sense. {"id": "68:27/q04", "question": "What does 'deprived' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the deprivation denotes the lost harvest and its benefits or their resulting destitution.", "positions": [{"id": "68:27/q04/p1", "position": "They lost the garden's crop, fruit, benefit, blessing, or expected good.", "reasons": "Muqatil says they recognized punishment; al-Tabari's own account speaks of denied benefit, and his report from Qatada calls it repayment by deprivation of the garden. {"id": "68:27/q05", "question": "Why were they deprived?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:27/q05/p1", "position": "Their wrongdoing, especially intending to deny the poor, brought deprivation as punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj, al-Wahidi's exegetes, Ibn al-Jawzi, and Ibn Ashur connect the lost fruit to withholding it from the poor. {"id": "69:1/q01", "question": "What does al-Ḥāqqah refer to, and what does its name convey?", "turns_on": "The explanations select different aspects of ḥaqq: certainty, disclosure, recompense, fulfillment, overcoming, or impending punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "69:1/q01/p1", "position": "It names the Resurrection or Hour of Judgment.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima, Ibn ʿAbbās and others identify it thus. Al-Kashshāf and al-Rāzī say knowledge is figuratively assigned to the Hour, though people learn. Al-Ālūsī applies this to disclosure and realization, but al-Kashf limits it to disclosure. Al-Qāshānī assigns the disclosure and establishment of realities to the major resurrection in his conditional inward reading."}, {"id": "69:1/q01/p4", "position": "It is the Hour when deeds, reckoning, reward and punishment become real or due.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Razzāq reports Qatāda on deeds falling due; al-Māwardī reports Qatāda and Yaḥyā ibn Sallām on reward and punishment. Islahi says divine promises and messengers' warnings prove true."}, {"id": "69:1/q01/p7", "position": "It overcomes false opponents of God's religion.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı transmit al-Azharī's derivation from prevailing in a dispute. Al-Jishumī reports that the day overpowers unbelievers; al-Biqāʿī says it makes truth prevail."}, {"id": "69:1/q01/p8", "position": "It is the appointed event or calamity due to befall a people.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Elmalılı report this; Elmalılı calls it close to the inevitable Hour."}, {"id": "69:1/q01/p9", "position": "It points to each person's particular due right.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports a more specific and compelling form of right; Elmalılı cites 'this is my own right.'"}, {"id": "69:1/q01/p10", "position": "It is named for believers' rightful fear of it.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī offers this explanation."}, {"id": "69:1/q01/p11", "position": "It also includes inevitable punishment of peoples rejecting their messenger.", "reasons": "Islahi says punishment follows after a messenger conclusively conveys truth, and anticipates punishment in the Hereafter."}, {"id": "69:1/q01/p12", "position": "It can refer to Quraysh's crushing defeat for opposing the Prophet.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu reports Ateş's view, prompted by the ensuing punished peoples."}, {"id": "69:1/q01/p13", "position": "It realizes everything unbelievers rejected in earthly life.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this view from JJ."}, {"id": "69:1/q01/p14", "position": "In an inward reading it can designate the minor resurrection, the inevitable Hour.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī distinguishes this minor resurrection from the major resurrection in which realities become known and established."}, {"id": "69:1/q01/p15", "position": "It is a gathering identified by participants saying that they were at the ḥāqqah.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports this anonymous explanation and calls it absurd."}]}

{"id": "69:1/q04", "question": "What effect does the abrupt opening and questioning create?", "turns_on": "The notes identify repetition and questioning, and the isolated name, as different devices.", "positions": [{"id": "69:1/q04/p1", "position": "It magnifies the event and evokes awe at what exceeds human knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and al-Rāzī say repeating the noun instead of a pronoun heightens awe, and no imagination encompasses the Hour. {"id": "69:1/q05", "question": "How is al-Ḥāqqah related to al-Qāriʿah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:1/q05/p1", "position": "Both designate Resurrection, while al-Qāriʿah evokes its terrifying blow.", "reasons": "Muqātil cites 69:4 and 101:1; al-Durr transmits Qatāda and Ibn Jurayj. {"id": "69:3/q01", "question": "How are the first mā and adrāka construed?", "turns_on": "Whether the analysis foregrounds the nominal interrogative clause or the underlying prepositional construction of darā.", "positions": [{"id": "69:3/q01/p1", "position": "The first interrogative mā is the subject and adrāka its predicate; the addressee is its first object.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī, Ālūsī, Bursawī, and Elmalılı give the subject–predicate analysis. {"id": "69:3/q05", "question": "What effect does the question produce?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize different features of the interrogative: awe, a jolt to attention, reproach, or an unfamiliar name.", "positions": [{"id": "69:3/q05/p1", "position": "It magnifies the Resurrection, evokes its terror, and conveys that its full reality exceeds imagination.", "reasons": "Muqātil points to its severity; al-Ṭabarī reports Qatādah; al-Qushayrī stresses gravity; al-Wāḥidī's language scholars say the Prophet knows it by description but is addressed as though he did not; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah invokes unknown horrors and details; al-Qurṭubī combines grandeur with incomplete knowledge. Al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Biqāʿī, Bursawī, Ālūsī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Asad, Iṣlāḥī, and Study Quran stress the limits of conception.
